My pandemic passion project was to better my health and ensure that my immune system can toughen out any sickness that may come my way. I did that through running which led me to compete in my first half-marathon. An integral component of my training was, of course, my Spotify playlist which consisted of comedy podcasts to numb the pain, a bunch of motivational mumbo jumbo from David Goggins about 'staying hard', and then John Mayer who's pandemic passion project is the topic of conversation.

---

## What this notebook is, and what was broken

The original analysis ran in two halves: Spotify audio features (`music_analysis.R`) and
Genius lyrics (`lyric_analysis.R`). Re-running it in 2026 surfaced four blockers, all fixed
here:

1. **Spotify's `/audio-features` endpoint is gone.** Retired 2024-11-27 for any app without
   pre-existing extended quota. The audio half is now driven from the `.rds`/`.csv` extracts
   captured in January 2022 — the data survives even though the endpoint doesn't.
2. **The Genius scraper is dead.** `getLyrics()` selected `//*[@id="lyrics-root"]/div[2]`;
   that node no longer exists and the page is behind a bot challenge. Lyrics are now loaded
   from the CSV extracts rather than re-fetched.
3. **A silent bug.** `lyric_analysis.R:219` had a bare `sobrock_playlist_lyrics <- ` with the
   next statement lines below, so R quietly assigned it `library(tidytext)`'s return value.
4. **Encoding damage and a null row.** The scrape left invalid UTF-8 in 186 of 191 rows, and
   one playlist track had no lyrics at all. Both are handled explicitly below instead of
   propagating into the token counts.

Two things were added rather than repaired: the audio half's **Bonferroni-corrected testing**
is now applied to the lyric half as well, and the single sadness scalar is replaced by the
**full ten-dimension NRC profile**.

> Lyrics are inputs only. Every output below is an aggregate statistic; no lyric text is
> printed, and the corpus stays out of version control (`.gitignore` excludes `*.csv`).

```{r libs}
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(tidytext); library(syuzhet); library(ggplot2)
```

## Data

```{r load}
read_lyrics <- function(p) read.csv(p, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")

alb <- read_lyrics("data/clean/sobrock_album_lyrics.csv")
pl  <- read_lyrics("data/clean/sobrock_playlist_lyrics.csv")
jm  <- read_lyrics("data/clean/jm_vs_sobrock.csv")

# FIX 4: drop the null-lyric row rather than letting it become a zero-word track
dropped <- sum(is.na(pl$lyrics) | trimws(pl$lyrics) == "")
pl <- pl %>% filter(!is.na(lyrics), trimws(lyrics) != "", genre %in% c("Sob", "Rock"))

corpus <- bind_rows(
  alb %>% mutate(grp = "Sob Rock"),
  pl  %>% mutate(grp = genre),
  jm  %>% filter(genre == "JohnMayer") %>% mutate(grp = "John Mayer (other)")
) %>% distinct(title, grp, .keep_all = TRUE)

cat("dropped null-lyric rows:", dropped, "\n"); table(corpus$grp)
```

## Audio features: the 2022 question, tested

The original conclusion was read off boxplots — Sob Rock sat inside the comparison IQR on
energy and loudness, but not on valence. Testing it puts a p-value on that.

```{r audio}
aud <- bind_rows(
  read.csv("data/sob_rock_album.csv",    stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>% mutate(grp = "Sob Rock"),
  read.csv("data/sob_rock_playlist.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>% mutate(grp = genre)
)
feats <- c("acousticness","danceability","energy","instrumentalness",
           "liveliness","loudness","speechiness","valence","tempo")
bonf_a <- 0.05 / length(feats)

audio_tests <- lapply(feats, function(f) {
  sr <- aud[[f]][aud$grp == "Sob Rock"]
  data.frame(feature = f,
             p_vs_Sob  = t.test(sr, aud[[f]][aud$grp == "Sob"])$p.value,
             p_vs_Rock = t.test(sr, aud[[f]][aud$grp == "Rock"])$p.value)
}) %>% bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(sig_Sob  = ifelse(p_vs_Sob  < bonf_a, "YES", "-"),
         sig_Rock = ifelse(p_vs_Rock < bonf_a, "YES", "-")) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("p_"), ~round(.x, 4)))
audio_tests
```

Valence is the whole finding: it separates Sob Rock from the sad set decisively and puts it
on top of the rock set. The album is not sad-sounding. It is a rock record.

## Lyrics: the 2022 method, replicated

The original chain, reproduced exactly — contraction expansion, tokenize, lemmatize against
`lexicon::hash_lemmas`, drop stopwords and vocal filler, then take each track's sadness ratio
as sad-word count over total words.

```{r tidy}
ck <- lexicon::key_contractions; hl <- lexicon::hash_lemmas
expand_contractions <- function(x) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(ck))) x <- gsub(ck$contraction[i], ck$expanded[i], x, ignore.case = TRUE)
  x
}

tidy_lyrics <- corpus %>%
  mutate(lyrics = expand_contractions(lyrics)) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, lyrics) %>%
  left_join(hl, by = c("word" = "token")) %>%
  mutate(word = ifelse(is.na(lemma), word, lemma)) %>% select(-lemma) %>%
  anti_join(get_stopwords(), by = "word") %>%
  filter(!word %in% c("ooh","ah","da","oh","uh"))

nrc <- get_sentiment_dictionary("nrc")
sad_words <- nrc %>% filter(sentiment == "sadness") %>% distinct(word) %>% mutate(sad = TRUE)

sentiments <- tidy_lyrics %>%
  left_join(sad_words, by = "word") %>%
  group_by(title, grp) %>%
  summarise(sadness = sum(sad, na.rm = TRUE) / n(), words = n(), .groups = "drop")

sentiments %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(sadness), 4),
            median = round(median(sadness), 4), sd = round(sd(sadness), 4))
```

By the group means Sob Rock looks like the saddest set in the study — above the sad
comparison songs and above Mayer's own back catalogue. That reading does not survive a test.

```{r lyric-test}
sr <- sentiments$sadness[sentiments$grp == "Sob Rock"]
lyric_tests <- lapply(c("Sob","Rock","John Mayer (other)"), function(g) {
  p <- t.test(sr, sentiments$sadness[sentiments$grp == g])$p.value
  data.frame(comparison = g, p = round(p, 4),
             sig = ifelse(p < 0.05/3, "YES", "-"))
}) %>% bind_rows()
lyric_tests

cat(sprintf("mean %.4f vs median %.4f, sd %.4f - driven by one track at %.3f\n",
            mean(sr), median(sr), sd(sr), max(sr)))
```

The mean is carried by a single outlier. Nothing is significant.

## Bolster: the full emotion profile

The 2022 version collapsed ten NRC dimensions into one scalar. Keeping all ten, scored per
track so each can be tested the way the audio features were.

```{r profile}
per_track <- tidy_lyrics %>%
  inner_join(nrc, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  count(title, grp, sentiment) %>%
  group_by(title, grp) %>% mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(title, grp, sentiment, share) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = share, values_fill = 0)

emos <- c("anger","anticipation","disgust","fear","joy",
          "negative","positive","sadness","surprise","trust")
bonf_e <- 0.05 / length(emos)

emo_tests <- lapply(emos, function(e) {
  s <- per_track[[e]][per_track$grp == "Sob Rock"]
  data.frame(emotion = e,
             p_vs_Sob  = round(t.test(s, per_track[[e]][per_track$grp == "Sob"])$p.value, 4),
             p_vs_Rock = round(t.test(s, per_track[[e]][per_track$grp == "Rock"])$p.value, 4),
             p_vs_JM   = round(t.test(s, per_track[[e]][per_track$grp == "John Mayer (other)"])$p.value, 4))
}) %>% bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(any_sig = ifelse(pmin(p_vs_Sob, p_vs_Rock, p_vs_JM) < bonf_e, "YES", "-"))
emo_tests
```

Ten emotions, three comparisons, thirty tests. At the corrected threshold of
`r round(0.05/10, 4)`, none of them separate Sob Rock from anything.

## The cross-instrument check

The two halves were never pointed at each other. If lyrical sadness and musical mood measure
the same underlying thing, they should agree track by track.

```{r cross}
joined <- sentiments %>%
  inner_join(aud %>% select(name, grp, valence), by = c("title" = "name", "grp" = "grp"))
ct <- cor.test(joined$sadness, joined$valence)
cat(sprintf("matched tracks: %d | Pearson r = %.3f, p = %.4f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            nrow(joined), ct$estimate, ct$p.value, ct$conf.int[1], ct$conf.int[2]))

joined %>% group_by(grp) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), lyric_sadness = round(mean(sadness), 4),
            audio_valence = round(mean(valence), 3))
```

```{r cross-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(joined, aes(valence, sadness, colour = grp)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = .85) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "grey40", linewidth = .6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Sob" = "#2F4C9B", "Rock" = "#BC4A2E", "Sob Rock" = "#17805C")) +
  labs(x = "Spotify valence (musical positivity)", y = "NRC sadness ratio (lyrics)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Two instruments, one object",
       subtitle = "Lyrical sadness and musical mood are uncorrelated across the corpus") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The correlation is indistinguishable from zero. And the group means run in opposite
directions: Sob Rock carries the highest lyrical sadness in the study *and* the highest
musical valence. The sob is in the words; the rock is in the music; neither instrument sees
both.

## What this cannot see

- **Power.** Ten tracks against thirty-odd, with a Bonferroni correction over ten emotions.
  A null here means the instrument cannot resolve the question at album scale — not that no
  difference exists. The honest ceiling of a ten-track album is low.
- **Bag-of-words has no irony.** NRC counts sad words wherever they appear. Mayer described
  the record as a shitpost; a lexicon cannot tell a sad song from a song wearing sadness as a
  costume, which is precisely the distinction this album is built on.
- **The comparison set is hand-picked.** The 35 sad and 35 rock tracks were chosen by me in
  2022. It is a reasonable set, not a random sample, and every result is conditional on it.
- **Audio features are a vendor's model.** `valence` was Spotify's proprietary estimate,
  never documented in full and now withdrawn. It cannot be audited or recomputed.
